cases.title: Static on Pier Nine
cases.tagline: A pledge night, a pirate broadcast, and a fired DJ everyone wants to blame.
cases.role: You volunteer one night a month as the signal analyst for KPIR 91.3, Pier Nine Radio. The station runs Google SecOps. You have read access to Search and nothing else.
opening: Pledge Night at Pier Nine Radio is the one night the station's phones never stop. At 03:10, between a jazz block and the overnight news, the playout system aired a segment nobody scheduled: a distorted voice reading the names of the night's biggest donors, one by one, followed by forty seconds of static.

By 03:14 the board treasurer, Hal Brunner, was in the control room. By 03:20 he had a suspect: Marco Vela, the overnight host the station let go last week, who still knows every password on the pier. Station manager Odalys Reyes is not ready to call anyone. 'Bring me what the logs say,' she tells you. 'Not what the room thinks.'
The station's events are in Google SecOps. You have until the morning news to work out what happened, in what order, and who needs to be told.

people.note: Runs the pledge desk, certain it was Marco.

people.name: Marco Vela
people.note: Let go last week. Account was disabled on his last day.

people.name: Priya Nair

people.name: Dez Okafor

people.name: Tomas Ikeda
people.note: Runs the board in Studio A.

systems.note: The playout PC. Whatever it is told to air, it airs.

systems.note: Two shared workstations at the pledge desk.

systems.note: Remote access gateway. Staff sign in from home through it.

cases.summary: Pledge Night. A pirate segment airs at 03:10, the board has a suspect, and the logs say something else.

cases.title: The week after
cases.tagline: The password is reset, the task is gone, the range is blocked. Did the fix hold, and is the path one story?
cases.role: You are back at the signal desk for the membership drive, one week after Pledge Night. Odalys applied every item on your Contain and Eradicate lists. You still have read access to Search and nothing else.
cases.summary: One week later, at the same station, after the fix. Subtler, quieter, and the question is whether the fix held; then, on Monday, whether the events are one story and who owns the hosts they touched.
opening: Friday, 18:00, the membership drive. The pledge-desk password was reset on Saturday morning, the PledgeSync task and its folder were removed, AUTOMATION-01 was rebuilt, and the gateway now blocks 203.0.113.0/24. Dez also wrote an allowlist of sponsor domains before lunch, by copying every sponsor-looking name out of last week's logs, so the station could tune out the known-good and see what was left.

Nothing airs that should not. No burst of failures, no encoded PowerShell, no forty-eight-megabyte upload. At 05:40 Odalys asks the only question that matters a week after an incident: did the fix hold? She wants it answered the way last week's brief was answered: from the records, with the records.
The station has twelve hours of its own logs again. The attacker, if they came back, had a week to read the same brief you wrote.

On Monday morning the ticket is still open. Before it closes, Odalys wants two things the Friday brief could not give her: proof that the gateway login and the file server are one story, written as a query someone can rerun, and the station directory beside every row, so each item of the fix has an owner.

people.name: Odalys Reyes

people.name: Hal Brunner
people.note: Still at the pledge desk. Did not click anything this week.

people.name: Priya Nair
people.note: Second drive. Also received this week's lure; did not open it.

systems.note: Remote access gateway. Hands each remote session an address from 10.9.4.200 upward.

systems.note: station_allowlist, a data table migrated from a reference list written in a hurry; also privileged_accounts, gateway_blocks and lookalike_shapes, and the legacy lists they replace. See the Lists and tables panel on the desk.

systems.note: The station's entity context: users with titles, roles and remote access, assets with owners and criticality, each record valid over a time range. See the Entities panel on the desk.

cases.title: A different pier
cases.tagline: A software update at a ferry co-operative, a disciplined deckhand, and a day to say which one took the manifests.
cases.role: You are the analyst Saltmarsh Ferries hired for one day, on the strength of the Pier Nine brief. Their events are in Google SecOps. You have read access to Search and the bundled directory, and nothing else. Nobody here will explain a query to you; the casebook is yours from Scope to Handoff.
cases.summary: A different organisation and a different shape: no phish, no stolen password. A vendor update that carried a passenger, a scheduled task, a beacon on a port nothing else uses, and a deckhand everyone suspects. Less guidance, the same discipline.
opening: Gull Pier, the other end of the harbour. Saltmarsh Ferry Co-operative runs three passenger boats, two ticket kiosks and a dispatch desk, all on one small network and one piece of software: TideWatch, which schedules sailings, sells tickets and keeps the passenger manifests. At 14:10 the vendor's security advisory arrives: build 4.7.2, pushed that morning from the vendor's own update server, was signed on a compromised build server and carries a plugin the vendor never wrote.

Operations manager Marguerite Doyle has a different theory. Rafael Quinn, a deckhand on a final warning, worked the dispatch desk alone from six until the dispatcher arrived, and the manifests live on that desk. 'He has had a grievance for a month,' she says. 'Tell me it wasn't him.'

The co-operative has ten hours of logs from 06:00 to 16:00 UTC and a volunteer IT lead, Theo Lindqvist, who has already read the advisory and looked at the dispatch host once. You have until the last sailing to say what happened, in what order, what left, and what the engineer should build so it cannot happen the same way twice.

bridge.title: Cybersecurity Engineering bridge
bridge.intro: Your Handoff ticket is where this course stops and an engineering course starts. An engineer picks it up and does four things with it, each of which is a change with an owner and a test, not a note.

items.heading: Controls from the Harden list
items.text: The TideWatch hosts get an egress allowlist (the vendor's update server and the fare processor, nothing else); the plugins folder gets application control so a binary the vendor did not sign cannot run from it; svc-tidewatch loses its read on \\FS-GULL\Manifests, which the dispatch client never needed; vendor updates install on one staging host and wait a day before the rest. Each control names the owner from the directory who will keep it true.

items.heading: Detections from chapter 11
items.text: The rules this handoff describes in words are written in Rule mode with their test cases: a host connecting to a new destination on a port the pier does not use, keyed by host over an hour (must fire DISPATCH-01 at 09:32, must not fire OFFICE-02); a scheduled task created by a service account within minutes of an installer; a service account reading the manifests share; an outbound connection over one megabyte from a dispatch host. Each carries its severity, its must-fire record from today and its must-not-fire key, and is replayed before it is approved.

items.heading: Acceptance tests
items.text: Every control and every rule gets a test the engineer runs and keeps: replay today's events and the beacon rule fires on the three hosts and not on the kiosks' fare traffic; copy tw-telemetry.exe into the plugins folder and it does not execute; run as svc-tidewatch and the manifests share returns access denied; the next vendor build reaches the staging host first and nowhere else for a day. A control without a test is a hope.

items.heading: What the next course does
items.text: It writes those controls and tests as configuration and code, reviews them the way chapter 11 reviewed a rule (against evidence, with a must-fire and a must-not-fire), and measures what the Pier Nine and Saltmarsh handoffs would have cost to prevent. The analyst's job ends at a ticket an engineer can act on; the engineer's job starts there.

boundary: Everything here is fiction: the station, the people, the logs, the addresses. Nothing runs against a real SIEM. Do not type real workplace values into this site; practise the shape of the query here and use real values only inside tools your employer authorizes.
